title: Lexical Scope in Action: Closure Captures Global y
description: A Scheme snippet showing define, lambda, and a call. The lambda captures y from the global environment at definition time, so rebinding y later would not affect the closure.
source: draft: opencode free model + edit: codex

steps.description: Line 1 defines y as 10 in the global environment. This creates a binding y=10 in the global frame.

Line 2 defines f as a lambda that takes x and returns (+ x y). The lambda becomes a closure: it stores its parameter list (x), its body (+ x y), and a pointer to the environment where it was defined (the global frame with y=10).

steps.question: When (f 5) runs on line 3, a new call frame is created with x=5 and outer pointing to the closure's saved environment (the global frame). The body (+ x y) evaluates. What value does y have, and why?
steps.answer: y is 10. The closure captured the global frame where y=10 at definition time. The call frame's outer points to that same global frame. Rebinding y after f is defined would create a new binding in the global frame, but the closure still sees the original binding through the chain  -  this is lexical scope.

steps.description: Line 3 calls f with argument 5. The call frame has x=5, outer points to the global frame (where y=10). x resolves to 5 locally, y resolves to 10 via outer. (+ 5 10) returns 15.
Run it. (define y 10) evaluates: global frame gets binding y=10.
(define f (lambda (x) (+ x y))) evaluates: the lambda creates a closure with params (x), body (+ x y), and env = global frame. Global frame gets binding f = that closure.

(f 5) evaluates: f is looked up in global frame, returns the closure. A new call frame is created with x=5, outer = closure's env (global frame). Body (+ x y) evaluates in call frame: x=5 locally, y=10 via outer. Result is 15.
